# Geoengineering prioritization: a study of a proposed expression of mitigation deterrence

- Open access
- Published: 23 October 2025

- Amanda Sie ORCID: orcid.org/0000-0002-3369-6054 1, 
- Steven R. Brechin ORCID: orcid.org/0000-0002-3426-4624 1 & 
- Christopher P. Borick ORCID: orcid.org/0000-0003-4850-119X 2 

## Abstract

Geoengineering (GE) represents technologies designed to address climate change, either through carbon dioxide removal or solar radiation management. Researchers and stakeholders worry GE technologies will distract the public’s and policymakers' attention away from supporting more proven climate mitigation strategies, creating a “mitigation deterrence” effect. Missing from the discussion is investigating who is more likely to support GE over all other climate actions in general. “GE prioritization” turns our attention to those who are supportive of focusing efforts on GE instead of mitigation and other climate actions. This group is understudied but potentially as concerning as mitigation deterrence in future contexts of climate policymaking. We use a unique dataset to explore the US public’s preferences for four GE technologies, and whether these preferences predict GE prioritization. We also explore social factors including political, environmental, and climate beliefs, and confidence in scientists to conduct GE. We use data from the Summer 2020 wave of the National Surveys on Energy and Environment, a nationally representative survey in the US, and employ multinominal logistic regressions to examine the factors that predict GE prioritization. We find that three GE technologies, ocean fertilization, ambient air capture, and space mirrors positively predicted GE prioritization, as does higher confidence in scientists, conservative political beliefs, and being non-White. We argue that individuals who prioritize GE may provide justification for mitigation deterrence at the policy level in the future, and that further research is needed to create a more complete model to understand why individuals prioritize GE.

## 1 Introduction

Global levels of greenhouse gases (GHGs) continue to rise, and climate scientists and policymakers are increasingly worried that the Paris Agreement’s goal of remaining within 1.5 degrees Celsius of preindustrial global temperatures will be surpassed. Given the growing crisis, scientists and policymakers are considering the role of geoengineering (GE) technologies in attaining target temperature goals. The technologies are organized into two categories: nature-based and mechanically engineered carbon dioxide removal (CDR), and solar radiation management (SRM), also called solar geoengineering. CDR aims to extract and store historical CO₂ emissions from the atmosphere, while SRM techniques reduce radiative forcing from the sun to temporarily lower global temperatures, but would not address the accumulation of atmospheric greenhouse gases (Royal Society 2009). Most CDR and SRM technologies are unproven at scale, and while they could provide stopgaps in global temperature rises, many have the potential for serious uninformed and unanticipated environmental and social consequences (see Sovacool 2021 for a comprehensive explanation of benefits and risks of proposed geoengineering options). Prior research shows that the general public’s support for GE technologies is low, as is their understanding of them.

A significant concern that arises with increased attention and research for GE is the “mitigation deterrence” problem, a type of moral hazard. Researchers and stakeholders hypothesize that pursuing CDR and SRM technologies might provide the appearance of relatively easy technological fixes to the climate change problem, thereby lessening the focus on vital GHGs reduction efforts and therefore failing to address the root cause of climate change (Lawrence and Crutzen 2017; Lin 2013; McLaren 2016). Some members of the public, policymakers, and the fossil fuel industry could present GE technologies as solutions to climate change to avoid the difficult political, economic and social transitions away from fossil fuels. They could do this by imagining a future in which we could simply reduce temperatures or remove the GHGs that we emit to minimize climate risks. Mitigation deterrence could exhibit itself both through changes in individual mitigation behaviors or reduced support for collective mitigation action and policies. There are others, however, who argue that GE could induce the opposite reaction, increasing support for current mitigation efforts. Learning about the serious possibility or the view that GE could be used to meet Paris Agreement goals might increase climate change risk perceptions and thus lead to greater mitigation support and efforts, i.e. “mitigation galvanization” (Cherry et al. 2021; Merk et al. 2016; Reynolds 2015; Wibeck et al. 2017). A small but growing literature examines whether and for whom a mitigation deterrence or mitigation galvanization response to GE may arise in behavioral and policymaking situations.

Much of this previous mitigation deterrence research, and even previous research on GE public opinion more generally, is missing an investigation into who is more likely to prioritize GE. It is one thing to reduce support for mitigation actions because of GE (i.e. mitigation deterrence), but it is another to prioritize GE deployment over mitigation and other climate actions. Although GE researchers and stakeholders have strongly advocated for ensuring that GE is developed using a “portfolio approach” of climate actions that centers and prioritizes mitigation, there will inevitably be groups who will advocate for the exact opposite. There may be people whose belief in climate change or support for mitigation is already low, but who may nonetheless support GE. We propose a new concept, “GE prioritization,” to capture this belief that GE is more important than GHG mitigation, adaptation, or other climate actions. Those who prioritize GE may eventually compel other individuals, institutions, or decision-makers towards mitigation deterrence or galvanization, depending on future political contexts and institutional arrangements of GE deployment.

In this paper, we investigate who prioritizes GE as the most important climate action. Within the US context, we explore the effects of a variety of climate and environmental beliefs and sociodemographic factors. Additionally, we attempt to identify if support for any specific GE technologies is related to GE prioritization. The characteristics of each GE approach may shape how or why someone prioritizes GE. One GE technology might induce higher perceptions of climate risk than another, reducing its level of public support. Or, a technology might appear more feasible, reducing the support for actual mitigation efforts, thus generating the potential for a moral hazard. Pinpointing the social and technological characteristics that determine GE prioritization will assist researchers and policymakers by providing more specific contexts for future mitigation deterrence or galvanization.

## 2 Background

### 2.1 Conceptualizing GE prioritization

Most of the literature on mitigation deterrence has been focused on whether individual members of the public will reduce their support for mitigation policies and action when they learn about the potential uses for GE to address climate change. Recent research findings on public expressions of moral hazard are inconclusive, with some researchers finding support for mitigation deterrence concerns (Campbell-Arvai et al. 2017; Corner and Pidgeon 2014; Raimi et al. 2019) while others do not (Cherry et al. 2021; Fairbrother 2016; Hart et al. 2022; Kahan et al. 2015; Merk et al. 2016). Some have found evidence that decision-makers are more likely to increase support for mitigation efforts when given the option to deploy GE technologies (Andrews et al. 2022; Cherry et al. 2022), and that the public’s acceptance of GE is conditioned upon ambitious emission reduction policies (Cox et al. 2020). Continued research and discussion on the mitigation deterrence vs. galvanization question are important, but they narrowly focus on two specific socio-psychological effects in relation to climate beliefs and policy support. On one hand, it makes sense to worry about whether GE will distract well-meaning stakeholders and decision-makers from GHG mitigation and a renewable energy transition, and it would be concerning if this also becomes the case for the general public. On the other hand, this may not be the most worrisome effect at all: what about those who, even without knowing much about GE, begin to claim that GE should be the top priority for all climate action?

Therefore, in this study we focus on “GE prioritization” as a potential roadblock to mitigation efforts. GE prioritization is not the same as individual-level mitigation deterrence, since we aren’t concerned about reduced mitigation support after learning about GE. Instead, we believe that it has the potential to lead to socio-political mitigation deterrence. Focusing on individual-level mitigation deterrence presumes that those who don’t already support climate mitigation are not a relevant group to climate action strategies, yet we also already know that climate inaction largely stems from both organized climate denial and misinformation, and a subsequent lack of prioritization from the general public (Brulle 2018; Dunlap 2013).

A contingent of the public who prioritizes GE might be more politically powerful than a public that reduces its support for mitigation. There are powerful forces at play that will most likely encourage GE’s use, especially if climate denialism loses its effectiveness as a strategy to slow the energy transition and decarbonization. Two rationales standout. The first is economic calculation. For over 30 years economists have debated the economic advantages of various climate policies, including GE. Nobel Laureate William Nordhaus conducted economic analyses of climate solutions with his famous DICE model (Nordhaus 1993, 2013), arguing that GE would be economically advantages over mitigation approaches. The decades since have produced much debate over the actual economic benefits of various solutions (see Hänsel et al. 2020). It is, however, plausible that a decision-maker may choose to deploy GE in order to reduce the pace of emission reductions when balancing costs of faster emission cuts against future climate risks (Keith 2021). The second rationale is the tremendous political-economic power of economic investments built upon our fossil fuel-based global economy. These powerful companies and support organizations have invested heavily in media framing and political lobbying to deny climate change (Brulle 2020) and will use GE as a means to delay future climate action to maintain the fossil fuel base of the global economy (Gould and Lewis 2025). Companies like Occidental Oil, Chevron, and Exxon have already begun funding research and companies focused on direct air capture and other CDR approaches, in line with earlier promotions for carbon capture and sequestration technologies (Stuart et al. 2020). It is very plausible that these groups will use GE to perpetuate climate inaction in all the same ways they have done before: through cultural and discursive means, political means, and policy and institutional means (Brulle and Aronczyk 2019; Carmichael and Brulle 2017).

The counter-climate change movement (CCCM)’s instrumentalization of GE will, however, be contingent on a receptive public. While they may succeed in aligning GE framings with existing CCCM efforts, people who typically do not prioritize mitigation may also reject GE for a wide range of reasons.
